newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Asian economic growth should continue - ADB economist.
newsitem.headline: Asian economic growth should continue - ADB economist.

text.p: Asia was the fastest-growing region last year, and growth, though slowing, should remain strong this year and next, the chief economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Thursday.

"Despite major shocks, both internal and external, the Asian economies as a group and individually continued to perform in a very robust manner," Vishvanath V. Desai, ADB chief economist, told a news conference.
The Manila-based institution issued individual studies on more than 24 countries in its annual outlook released on Thursday.
Growth in the region slowed to 7.4 percent in 1996 from 8.2 percent the previous year and is expected to stabilise at about 7.4 percent in 1997 and 1998, the bank said.
However, Asia remains home to most of the world's poor, the bank said.
"There is a danger that the world, mesmerised by the overall economic performance of developing Asia will forget that the vast majority of the world's poor live in Asia," the bank said.
The report defined as poor anyone with an income of less than US$1 a day.
Since the 1970s, overall economic growth and labour productivity in Asia have outstripped those of Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa. Asia has more than half the world's labour force.
But the performance across the region has been far from uniform. The bank singled out South Asia, whose more than 515 million poor far exceed the total for Africa and Latin America.
"The differential has been so stark that it has virtually created two Asias -- dynamic and vibrant East Asia and slow South Asia," the report said.
The ADB cited a sharp drop in export growth, particularly in electronics, and the dollar's appreciation against the yen as part of the reason for declining growth in the region.
Desai said the "tremendous slowdown" in worldwide imports reduced export growth in all Asian economies except Vietnam.

Thailand saw no increase in exports last year, compared to 30 percent growth in 1995, he said, while China's export growth plunged to one percent from 25-26 percent and South Korea's fell to four percent from 25 percent a year earlier.
The region's overall export growth declined to six percent in 1996 from 23 percent in 1995, he said.
"Despite such a severe decline in the region, gross domestic product growth continued to be fairly high," Desai said.
World trade would regain its momentum this year, he said.
But growth of electronics exports may continue slowing as fewer new products come on to the market, the bank said.
"In the absence of major new products coming on stream, the industry is unlikely to return to its pre-1996 boom years," the bank said.
The bank said regional economies must come up with their own ideas instead of relying on imported technology if they are to maintain the meteoric growth rates of the past few years.

"In the early stages of industrialisation, it may be perfectly sensible to rely on imported technology rather than innovation. However, as economies catch up, then an indigenous capacity to innovate becomes more important," the bank said.
